newsitem.title: GERMANY: German opposition seeks ways to unite against Kohl.
newsitem.headline: German opposition seeks ways to unite against Kohl.

text.p: Tired of playing the eternal outsiders, Germany's left-of-centre opposition parties are searching as never before for a common front to finally push veteran Chancellor Helmut Kohl from power.
The Social Democrats (SPD) and ecologist Greens lead Kohl's centre-right coalition in the opinion polls and have two years before the next general election in late 1998.
But the rivalries between the two parties run so deep that betting on them winning is still a risky business. It is not even clear they will join forces for the decisive battle.
Even if they do, opinion polls show, the weakness of the larger SPD could turn out to overshadow the growing strengths of the smaller Greens.
"We need a new constellation, we need a change of power," SPD party manager Franz Muenterfering declared on Monday.
Asked if that meant a coalition with the Greens, though, Muenterfering would only say: "The Greens will be an option for possible cooperation with the SPD."

At their annual congress over the weekend, the once-radical Greens renewed their long-standing call for a "red-green" front to challenge Kohl and steered the party further towards the political centre to make it a credible partner for government.
But delegates also hailed as their new hero Rezzo Schlauch, the Greens leader who humiliated the SPD in the mayor's race in Stuttgart last month.

Schlauch swept almost 40 percent of the vote, four points behind the Christian Democrat (CDU) who won City Hall but a full 20 points ahead of the trounced SPD. Among voters under 50, he won more votes than any of his rivals.
Strongest at the local level, the Greens are also gaining ground on the SPD in cities like Berlin, Frankfurt and Hamburg.

Latest national opinion polls put the SPD at 35 percent and the Greens at 13 percent. This 48 percent total contrasts with the 45 percent recorded for Kohl's CDU (40 percent) and its Free Democratic Party partner (five percent).
But the SPD faces a dilemma. Red-green coalitions already tested out at the state level have usually been strained and ended up boosting support for the Greens.
The SPD displayed its concerns unmistakably last week when it devoted its annual congress to the single issue of how to win back the young voters streaming to the Greens.

The party, a magnet for youth in the early 1970s, decked the hall with graffiti-style posters. Oskar Lafontaine, the former enfant terrible who is now the party's plump 53-year-old chairman, wriggled with young dancers on the main stage.
But the SPD's youth wing wrote off the strained effort to look "Young and Cool", as the posters proclaimed.

"When well-meaning party functionaries go to a techno party, it's about as believable as when Boris Yeltsin, with his heart disease, dances rock and roll at an election rally," SPD youth leader Andrea Nahles, 25, complained.

In a gesture that raised eyebrows in Bonn, the head of Germany's DGB trade union association Dieter Schulte addressed the Greens congress -- the first time the traditionally pro-SPD unions have officially met the ecologists.

Schulte, who all but ignored the SPD earlier this year in a vain bid to forge an "Alliance for Jobs" with Kohl, made clear the unions no longer saw the Greens as a pampered middle class more interested in saving forests than creating jobs.

"We now have more in common that just the belief that we have an incompetent government in Bonn," he said. "We should continue to work on this without either of us placing too many demands on the other. We're ready to do that."
